name: DSpatch development loop (runnable subset)
purpose: The implement, verify, review and rework part of the DSpatch development loop, as a loop DSpatch itself can walk against a project that is not DSpatch. One bounded assignment per run: the coordinator establishes what it means and briefs the implementer, the implementer carries it out, an independent verifier checks it by means that suit it, an independent reviewer reads the account and the evidence together, and the coordinator reports. Most assignments here are a change to the code, and where one is, the commands and their exit codes are what evidence means; an assignment whose result is an answer, an analysis or an activity carried through to its end is the same five steps with the working folders unchanged at the end of them.
notes:
IT IS NOT OUR LOOP. It is a loop shaped like ours, running against another project. Our development loop runs in Cursor, through subagents, driven by a person; dspatch-development-loop.graph.json is the drawing of that and stays the truthful one. This file is the subset of it that DSpatch can actually walk, and it exists so that the standalone definition under dspatch-loop-definition is runnable rather than only drawable. Read the two together: this one is what runs, the other is what we do.

THE ROLES ARE NOT COPIED. Every node points at the role source in the DSpatch working copy that the .cursor/ agent files are generated from — docs/loop/roles/*.role.md — so there is exactly one place each role is maintained, and a role source states its own targets and requirements instead of having them inferred from a generated file's front matter. The standalone definition reaches all of them through its resourceRoot, and that dependency is declared there and shown on the row before the loop is chosen.

THE COORDINATOR IS A DIFFERENT ROLE FROM THE CURSOR ONE, and until DSP-83 it was not. Both coordinator nodes pointed at .cursor/skills/dspatch-loop/SKILL.md, which is the governance document for a coordinator sitting in a Cursor chat: it tells its reader to call five named subagents with Cursor's agent tool, to own a backlog card and a run journal, and to choose which specialist goes next. An agent inside a graph DSpatch walks does none of that — the runner opens the sessions, sends the briefs, files the results, picks the next node and stops at the bounds — so the file was instructing the step to do the run engine's job with the run's own bounded calls. docs/loop/roles/run/dspatch-run-coordinator.role.md is the same responsibility written for the side of the fence it is actually on, and it says in its own text how it differs. SKILL.md is unchanged: it is the entry point for the Cursor loop that develops DSpatch and that loop is still running. The role lives under roles/run/ rather than roles/ for the reason roles/project/ does: npm run roles:generate reads only the top level, and a role for an agent inside a DSpatch run is not a Cursor project agent and must not become one.

WHAT THIS SUBSET LEAVES OUT, and each omission is a node kind the runner cannot honour rather than a part of the work we think unimportant. (1) The three human nodes. niclas-mandate, niclas-decision and niclas-assessment stop a run and wait, and a run reaching one cannot be answered in the chat. Here the mandate IS the run — the text a person sent is what starts it, which is the same act niclas-mandate draws — and the two later ones are terminals: needs-a-decision ends the run where the drawing would have asked, and there is no node standing between the report and a person because in this loop a person reads the report. (2) The router. route-next-step is where the coordinator classifies what the step needs, and the runner takes a router's first declared outcome, so it would answer "plan" every time. The classification stays with the coordinator, which is why the coordinator node is the entry and the routing it does is implicit in this smaller shape. (3) Planning. backlog-planner and plan-review are left out with it, because a plan proposal is about a backlog DSpatch neither owns nor can write. (4) The candidate. consumes hands over a report, not the tree the report was about, so "the verifier checks the same tree the implementer changed" is true only because the run is sequential over one working copy — nothing here binds a verdict to a revision.

WHAT IT KEEPS, and these are the things worth having. The five roles and the division of responsibility between them. A written brief to every step, because every step is its own agent with no sight of the others. Independent verification after implementation, and independent review of the implementer's account and the verifier's evidence together. A bounded rework round back to the implementer's own agent. Declared failures that route rather than stop: a wrong premise or a blockage ends the run at a terminal that says so, and a research need goes to the researcher and comes back.

WHO WRITES A REPORT. The runner does, for every step. Our Cursor loop asks the implementer and the verifier to write their own report file before they end, and that instruction exists because a chat message was lost on 14 September 2026 and the file on disk was the only thing that survived. It is a workaround for a transport, not a property of the work: here the step's own account is the result, the runner files it at the archive path and checks that it arrived, and a machine check beats an instruction in a document. The two read-only roles could not write one anyway. So report.writtenBy names the coordinator throughout, which is who owns the archive in our loop too.

WHAT AN ASSIGNMENT MAY BE, and this is DSP-101. Most runs of this loop change code, and where one does, every field down the middle still asks for the commands and the exit codes; none of that is softened here. What changed is that the fields no longer *presume* it. Until 22 September 2026 they all did: the coordinator was to brief "the bounded change", the implementer to report "what you changed and why", the reviewer to read the account against "the actual code". So a mandate whose whole point was that the folders stay untouched — walk the graph so the animations can be filmed — had no shape of brief to be written in, and the coordinator wrote it one that fitted the fields instead of the assignment: "Create a temporary test scenario that demonstrates the liveness animation sequence in the MiniDAWLab project". The meaning was gone at the first step and no later step could recover it. The texts now ask for the piece of work and name the change as one kind of it.

Nothing here recognises a category of request. There is no rule about demonstrations, none about liveness, none about trivial or empty tasks, and no branch that behaves differently because of what a mandate is about. The drawing simply stopped asserting something that was only ever true of most assignments, and a run that correctly ends with nothing changed now has the same five steps and the same evidence rules as any other.

WHAT A STEP HAS TO SAY FOR THE RUN TO ROUTE IT, and this is DSP-102. Three steps down the middle — coordinator, implementer, verifier — declare their own outcomes, so each of them must name its result and a reply that names none is no longer read as one. That was the defect: outcomes has always meant this step must name its result and the runner has always refused to let such a node finish on plain success, and these three simply did not carry the field, so for them success was the residue of every reply that was not a declared failure, and the message told them so — a step that finished writes no such line. Nothing about the general routing changed to fix it; the drawing changed.

Each of the three names its success first and a name for did not establish it second, and each says in whenUndeclared which of its own names a reply that declares none is routed on. So a reply with no name takes e01c, e02a or e09a to stopped, which is a route this drawing chose. The alternative was available and was considered: a node declaring only its success name would fault the run instead, the way implementation-review does today. Niclas chose the graceful route knowing the cost. Nothing here reads prose for a token and nothing asks a model what a reply meant: the route is taken on the absence of a form, not on an opinion about the text, so a question, a bold refusal and a polite essay are the same thing to it.

That gives stopped a third cause, and it is a real addition to the vocabulary of endings rather than a tidy-up. Its purpose now says so, and says what it must not be read as: a step can do the work perfectly and still not name a result, so arriving here is not a verdict on the work. The step's report is filed before the route is chosen, so what it did and what it actually said survive whichever edge is taken.

WHICH NAME IS A ROUTE, AND WHY IT IS WRITTEN DOWN, and this is DSP-103. The sentence above used to end differently: the second name was spelled unclear or could-not-check because those two literals were the whole of what the engine's fallback recognised, so these three nodes had the graceful route by virtue of a spelling, a node that called the same idea not-established stopped the run instead, and no part of the drawing or the node panel said any of it. Every node that wants that route now states it in whenUndeclared, naming one of its own outcomes; a node that states nothing stops the run, which is exactly what a node without one of the two words already did. No outcome name carries behaviour in either direction any more, and renaming an outcome here is now a visible edit to this field rather than a silent change of where a non-answer goes.

researcher changed with it and is no longer left permissive — see that node's own notes for why plain success was the wrong contract for it. coordinator-report was left as it was, because it was DSP-97's own subject; that card has now been decided and the next section is it.

WHAT THIS LOOP SAYS WHEN THE WORK WAS ACCEPTED AND THE RUN COULD NOT REPORT ON IT, and this is DSP-97. coordinator-report declared no outcomes and no failures, so it had no routable way to say it could not do its own step. One narrow path followed: a report step that filed a report saying it could not report still produced plain success, took e14 and reached delivered, whose ending is success. Only the tick was wrong — the recorded outcome was verification-not-performed either way, runOutcomeFrom never reads terminalNodeId, and the badge and its sentence were honest — but the tick was ahead of the facts. The worst case was already caught and still is: produces.required means a step that files nothing faults and reaches no terminal.

The destination is reporting-incomplete, labelled Ended without complete reporting, and Niclas decided its register as well as its wording. It states what happened and nothing more. It does not assert the work is done — not because a report is missing, and not because there are files in the folder, since a missing report is a missing report and files in a folder are files in a folder, and either reading would be DSpatch claiming something it cannot know. The reason is preserved in the step's own report, which is filed before the route is chosen, and in the recorded outcome, whose provenance says whether the step named the result or DSpatch read the absence of one (DSP-102 and DSP-103 did that half). Evidence about work that was completed is stated separately from the ending, so a reader sees the two and judges.

implementation-review shares that destination and keeps its own reason. Its three verdicts are untouched and route exactly as they did; what it gained is could-not-review, for the case where the reporting contract this node sets it cannot be fulfilled at all, and a whenUndeclared naming it. That closes the second half of the same gap: this node declared no failures either, so a reviewer that could not answer — or that wrote its whole review in prose and never put a verdict on the line the message asked for — was an undeclared product and stopped the run as a runtime fault one step from the end. Shared destination, distinct reason: the edges are e13a and e14a, the outcome names differ, and the path says which node the run came from.

What this did not do. delivered is not relabelled and its purpose is unchanged. No terminal was redesigned and no new kind of ending was introduced: TerminalEnding still has two values and this one is not-success, because that field answers only the question the green tick asks and the reasons live in the terminal's purpose where they cannot disagree with a second vocabulary. No mechanism was added to the engine — outcomes, whenUndeclared, an outcome edge and a terminal's ending are all of it — and nothing anywhere reads a report body, or infers a missing report from prose, to decide where a run ends.

STILL NOT HONOURED. limits are declared and not enforced; no-subagent-delegation and no-file-writes are honoured by the role text and not by the platform; nothing here survives a restart; and this drawing has never been walked against a real provider.

limits.note: The defaults in docs/DEVELOPMENT_LOOP.md, kept so that a run of this subset is bounded the way ours is. Declared and not enforced beyond what the runner counts: maxCalls and maxReworkRounds are counted and stop the run, maxTasks holds by construction because a run is one assignment.

archive.notes: Relative, and deliberately short: the base is the run-scoped folder DSpatch owns, so this names a directory inside that run and not a place in anybody's repository. A definition that borrowed DSpatch's roles and then wrote its reports into the DSpatch repository would be the collapse the resource root exists to prevent, arriving from the other side.

failureKinds.label: specification error
failureKinds.meaning: The assignment rests on a premise that turned out to be wrong. It cannot be corrected in place, and inventing a different assignment is worse than stopping.

failureKinds.label: research needed
failureKinds.meaning: A real uncertainty blocks the next step and the code to hand does not settle it. A bounded investigation comes before another attempt at the same change.

failureKinds.label: blocked
failureKinds.meaning: A concrete obstacle prevents meaningful progress: missing access, a blocking technology, or a decision this run cannot make.

nodes.label: Coordinator: establish and brief
nodes.purpose: Establish what this run's mandate actually asks, then write the brief the implementer works from: the bounded piece of work, what is deliberately outside it, and what would count as done. Where the mandate asks for a change to the working folders, say which change, what must not change with it, and what a verifier could run against it. Where it asks for something else — an answer, a calculation, an analysis, or an activity carried through to its end — brief that, and say what having done it looks like; do not turn it into a change so that it has a familiar shape, because the brief is all the later steps get and a change nobody asked for is the assignment replaced rather than specified. Do none of the work yourself — that is the implementer's step, and the later steps see only what you write here.

produces.note: The brief, whole. Every later step is a different agent with none of this conversation, and what you write here is what the implementer is given about the assignment.

nodes.notes:
The entry, and it is where the drawn niclas-mandate and route-next-step both land. The mandate is the text the person sent, so approval is the act of starting rather than a step; and classifying what the work needs is judgement, which is this role's, not a diamond the runner can resolve. Its role is the in-run coordinator (DSP-83), not the Cursor coordinator skill: see this graph's own notes for why those are two roles rather than one.

declaredFailures arrived with DSP-91 and closes a defect that cost a whole run. This node declared none, while the prompt asked every step for SPEC_ERROR and BLOCKED unconditionally — so on 21 September 2026 a coordinator that read its mandate, refused it and closed with RESULT: BLOCKED was routed as SUCCESS down e01, and the implementer was handed a refusal as its brief. The two edges below are where that refusal now goes. A coordinator is the one step that can see the assignment before any of the run's other calls are spent, so it is the cheapest place in the drawing to stop.

DSP-101 is in the purpose above, and this node is where that defect did its damage. This is the step that decides what the rest of the run is working on, and while its purpose asked for "the bounded change" there was one kind of assignment it could not write down — and what a step cannot write down, it converts. See this graph's own notes under WHAT AN ASSIGNMENT MAY BE for the run that showed it.

The outcomes line is DSP-102. Until 22 September 2026 this step's contract was that its ordinary reply was its brief, and it had no way of being wrong about that: with no outcomes declared, every reply that is not a declared failure means success. Naming briefed makes a brief a positive signature instead of a residue, and unclear gives a reply that named nothing somewhere honest to go — e01c — rather than stopping the run on what reads like a wiring fault. briefed is first because an unscripted dry run takes the first declared outcome, and this graph's ordinary path is walked that way.

nodes.label: Implementer
nodes.purpose: Do the bounded piece of work the brief describes and check it yourself. Where it is a change to the working folders, make it and run the real commands on it. Where the brief asks instead for an answer, a calculation, an analysis or an activity carried through to its end, produce that and leave the folders as you found them — a step that correctly changes nothing has finished its work, not skipped it. Your checks do not replace the independent verification that follows; say what you did, what you ran and what is still wrong.

limits.note: A wall-clock bound is how the runner notices a step that stopped moving. It is not a route: nothing in this graph is taken when it expires — see onRuntimeFault.

produces.note: What you did and why — the change you made, or the answer, analysis or activity the brief asked for instead — the commands you ran with their exit codes, and what is still wrong. Where the work was a change to the code, the commands and their exit codes are not optional and an account without them is not one. It is filed for you, in the run's own storage and not in the folders you are working in, and it is what the verifier and the reviewer are given, so anything they need has to be in it.

nodes.notes:
Revisited on a rework round, and the runner returns to this node's own agent — the same implementer, told what the review said, rather than a stranger handed a second attempt at someone else's work.

That sentence was written before anything made it true and stood untrue for a month: the run returned to the right agent and told it nothing, because consumes below is one list whatever edge arrives. What makes it true is on the edges now — e12 delivers the review, e06 delivers the research answer — and consumes is what a first visit gets, when no earlier step of this run has anything to say beyond the brief.

The outcomes line is DSP-102, and this is the node the observation was about. On 22 September 2026 this step was offered RESULT: blocked, asked a question instead, and was routed down e02 as a step that had finished — not because anything misread it, but because with no outcomes declared anything that is not a declared failure is success, and its message said as much in as many words: a step that finished writes no such line. done and unclear replace that residual contract with a positive one. A reply that names nothing takes e02a now, which is a route this drawing chose rather than a fault in the machinery. done is first because an unscripted dry run takes the first declared outcome.

nodes.label: Researcher
nodes.purpose: Investigate one bounded question and gather the evidence a decision needs, keeping what you observed apart from what you only read: missing measurements are unknown, not zero. In this graph the question is the one that stopped the implementation, which is this node's place in the loop rather than a limit on what the role can be asked.

produces.note: The evidence and what it settles. Read-only, so the runner files it for you.

nodes.notes:
Reached only from the implementer's research-needed failure, which is a routed decision and not a broken step. It is handed the implementer's account as well as the brief, which is where the question it is being asked actually is — see e03. The gap this note used to describe was real and is closed: consumes could not ask for the implementer's report, because consumes is asked on every arrival and would then have demanded on a first visit something only a later one could have; the arrival asks instead, and only the arrival that can answer.

The outcomes line is DSP-103, and this node was left permissive by DSP-102 as the cheapest case to leave alone. It is not the cheapest case: e06 returned on plain success, and with no outcomes declared every reply that is not a declared failure is plain success — so a researcher that asked a question back, or that investigated honestly and could not settle the matter, was handed to the implementer as finished research with its own uncertainty invisible in the routing. answered and not-established are that difference, said positively. Both go back to the implementer, because either way the work resumes where it stopped and the researcher's own account is what it resumes with; what changes is that the implementer is told which it is. answered is first because an unscripted dry run takes the first declared outcome.

This is a choice this drawing makes about this node. Nothing in the engine knows what a researcher is, no route here follows from the role's name, and a graph that used the same role at three nodes could give each of them a different contract.

nodes.label: Verifier
nodes.purpose: Check the work as it now stands and report evidence and gaps. Where the assignment was to change the code, that means running the real commands and giving their exit codes. Where its result is an answer, an analysis or an activity, check that against what was asked by means that suit it — and that the folders were left as the assignment said, which is a fair check; taking an inventory of them to decide what to check is not. Do not fix anything: an implementation you repaired is no longer the one that was handed to you.

produces.note: PASS / FAIL / NOT_RUN per claim, with the commands you ran and their exit codes wherever running something is what checked it. A claim nothing can be run against still needs the evidence you do have, named as what it is. An agent narrative is not evidence. It is filed for you, in the run's own storage and not in the folders you are working in.

nodes.notes:
Its own session, so it did not watch the implementation happen. What it knows about the work is the mandate, its own purpose and the implementer's report, which is what consumes hands it — and the working copy itself, which it can read.

The outcomes line is DSP-102. In the same 22 September 2026 run this step was offered RESULT: blocked, wrote BLOCKED in bold in the middle of its prose, and never put it on the line it was asked for — and nothing could notice, because its compliance was defined negatively. checked and could-not-check define it positively. Neither name is its PASS/FAIL: that still lives in its report and still reaches the reviewer whichever way it falls, which is why this node has no verdict branch and still does not. They say whether it was able to check at all. whenUndeclared above is what makes a reply that declares nothing route on e09a instead of stopping the run; until DSP-103 that followed from could-not-check being one of two spellings the engine recognised, which was a routing decision this drawing never actually made.

nodes.label: Implementation review
nodes.purpose: Read the implementer's account and the verifier's evidence together, against the assignment — and against the actual code where the assignment was to change it — and answer accept, rework or needs-decision with the reasons behind it. What you are judging is the assignment that was given: where it asked for an answer, an analysis or an activity rather than a change, unchanged working folders are the assignment honoured and not a delivery that is missing. Accept only what the evidence supports; a check nobody ran is unknown, not a pass.

produces.note: ACCEPT, REWORK or NEEDS_DECISION against the assignment, the verifier's evidence, and the actual code where the assignment concerned it, with the reasons. Read-only, so the runner files it.

nodes.notes:
An agent node and not a gate. A gate in this runner starts the project's own command, which is the wrong mechanism for a judgement: it would reach no reviewer, build no brief and use none of what this node consumes. A verdict of rework is an outcome and not a failure — the reviewer did its job and the answer was no — and maxReworkRounds is what stops the same assignment being handed to more agents.

The fourth outcome is DSP-97 and it is not a fourth verdict. accept, rework and needs-decision are what this step answers about the work, and they keep the edges they have always had. could-not-review is what it says when the contract this node sets it — a verdict against the assignment, the evidence and the code, with the reasons — cannot be fulfilled at all, which is a different kind of statement and goes to a different place: e13a, to the ending that says the run finished without complete reporting and says nothing else. Niclas settled that the two nodes share that destination and keep distinct reasons, so the name here is this node's own and not the report step's.

whenUndeclared is the half that closes the gap the card was filed for. Until DSP-97 this node declared outcomes and stated no fallback, so a reply naming none of the three — including a reviewer that wrote its whole reasoning in prose and never put a verdict on the line the message asked for — was an undeclared product and stopped the run as a runtime fault at the second-to-last step. It now takes the same route as an explicit could-not-review, and the recorded outcome's provenance is what tells them apart: step-declared where the step named it, engine-fallback where DSpatch routed on the absence of a name. Nothing reads the prose for a verdict, here or anywhere: the route is taken because a form the message asked for is missing.

nodes.label: Coordinator: report
nodes.purpose: Summarise what was done, what was checked and what remains, as copyable text a person can answer in one pass. Lead with what the run produced: what is now true of the project where it changed something, and the answer, the analysis or the activity itself where that was what was asked for. Name the commands the evidence came from, and keep what was observed apart from what was claimed.

produces.note: The run's report, as copyable Markdown. It is the last thing written and it is what a person reads instead of the journal.

nodes.notes:
The outcomes line is DSP-97, and until 30 September 2026 this node was the last one left without it — deliberately, because what this loop should say when the work was accepted and the run could not report on it was an authoring decision nobody had made. Declaring nothing had one consequence and it was narrow: a report step that filed a report saying it could not do its own step still produced plain success, took e14 and reached delivered, whose ending is success. Nothing else was wrong on that path. The recorded outcome was still verification-not-performed, runOutcomeFrom never reads terminalNodeId, and the badge and the sentence beside it were honest. The green tick on Delivered was the whole of it, and it was ahead of the facts.

reported and could-not-report replace that residual contract with a positive one, and reported is first because an unscripted dry run takes the first declared outcome. This is the same shape DSP-102 gave the three steps down the middle; what differs is where the second name goes. Not stopped: the premise was not wrong, the work was not blocked, and the review accepted — so all three of that terminal's sentences would be untrue here. Not needs-a-decision: the review already answered, and there is nothing to decide. reporting-incomplete is the ending this card adds, and it states what happened and refuses to state anything else.

whenUndeclared names could-not-report, so a reply with no such line takes e14a rather than stopping the run as a fault at the very last step, and the recorded outcome says which of the two it was — step-declared where the step named it, engine-fallback where DSpatch read the absence of a name. Nothing here reads the report body. The worst case is unchanged and is still caught elsewhere: produces.required is true, so a step that files nothing at all faults with required-result-missing and reaches no terminal of any kind.

nodes.label: Delivered
nodes.purpose: The assignment was carried out, verified, reviewed and reported — the change, where one was asked for, and the answer, analysis or activity where that was the assignment. Whether the backlog task is done is a person's judgement on the criteria, not this run's.

nodes.label: Needs a decision
nodes.purpose: The review found something the run cannot settle: product direction, a mandate it does not have, or a judgement no agent check stands in for. What the run produced is in its own record, and in the working copy too where the work changed something there; the reasons are in the review's report.

nodes.label: Ended without complete reporting
nodes.purpose: A step that owed a result in the form its own node asks for ended without one, so the run ends here, and that is the whole of what arriving here says. It does not assert that the work was done, and it does not assert that it was not. A report that is missing is a report that is missing; files in the working folders are files in the working folders; neither of those is something this run can read a delivery out of, and an ending that claimed one would be DSpatch saying something it cannot know. The actual reason is preserved and it is not in this sentence: the step's own account is filed before this route is chosen, and the recorded outcome says whether the step named this itself or whether DSpatch routed on the absence of a name. Evidence about work that was completed is stated separately from this ending — in the earlier steps' own reports, and in the working copy where the work changed something there — so that a person can read the two and judge between them. Two steps arrive here and their edges say which: the reporting step could not report, or the review could not answer with a verdict.
nodes.notes:
DSP-97, and Niclas settled the wording: described factually as ended without complete reporting, not asserting the work is done, the actual reason preserved and any evidence about completed work stated separately from the ending itself.

WHY IT IS A NEW TERMINAL. The three that already exist each say something this arrival cannot. delivered is the assignment carried out, verified, reviewed and reported, and a run that could not report has not done the last of those; relabelling it was ruled out and it is untouched. needs-a-decision is the review finding something the run cannot settle, and on the path that matters most here the review accepted. stopped is the premise being wrong, the work being blocked, or a step answering unroutably — and on the coordinator-report path the premise held, nothing was blocked, and the work was completed, verified and accepted and is in the working copy. Arriving here is none of those three, so a fourth ending is the honest answer and it is this loop's own vocabulary, not a change to the engine.

WHY ITS ENDING IS not-success. TerminalEnding has two values and this needs no third: the field answers only the question the green tick asks, and the reasons why a run ended are deliberately kept out of it so that they live in one place — the terminal's own purpose and RunOutcomeKind — rather than in two that can disagree. not-success is therefore the whole of what this field has to say, and it is stated rather than omitted, because an absent ending means the author has not said and the author has.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT WHAT A RUN RECORDS: nothing. Arriving at a terminal earns no verification, runOutcomeFrom never reads terminalNodeId, and this subset draws no gate, so a run reaching here records exactly what a run reaching delivered records. What the ending decides is the mark on the drawing, and on this one there is no tick.

nodes.label: Stopped without a result
nodes.purpose: The premise was wrong, the work was blocked, or a step answered in a form the run could not route. This is not a failure of the project and not a pass. The third cause is not a verdict on the work either: a step can do exactly what it was asked and still not name its result in the form its own message asked for, and the run ends here rather than reading a missing name as work delivered. What was tried and what is needed are in the step's own report, which is filed before the route is chosen — so where only the naming was missing, the work itself is in that report.

edges.label: the premise was wrong
edges.notes: DSP-91. Before this edge existed the coordinator had nowhere to refuse to, and a refusal was read as a brief.

edges.label: no brief was named
edges.notes: DSP-102. Where a reply arrives without the line that says this step produced a brief. Nothing reads the text for a reason: the route is taken because a form the message asked for is absent, and no opinion is formed about the words that are there. The reply is filed before this edge is chosen, so whatever the step actually said — a question, a refusal, an essay — is in the record for a person to read.

edges.label: the change, and its own checks
research needed first
edges.notes: DSP-95, closed as part of DSP-100. The researcher's own consumes is the brief alone, which is the whole assignment and not the question — so before this line the researcher was sent to investigate a bounded question nobody had told it. The implementer's report is where the question actually is: a step that declares research-needed still files what it was to file, so its account of where it stopped exists by the time this edge is taken. Both, because the question needs the assignment around it to be answerable.

edges.label: no result was named
edges.notes: DSP-102, and the edge the 22 September 2026 run needed and did not have. Without it a step that asked a question instead of naming a result went down e02 as work delivered, and by the reviewer's turn two non-results had been filed as results. The run stops at this step instead, one call in, with the step's own words filed.

edges.label: the question was answered
edges.notes:
The other half of e03. Work resumes where it stopped, so what comes back has to be the answer to the question that stopped it — the brief alone would return the implementer to the same blocked position with nothing new, which is the shape of defect DSP-100 was filed for.

DSP-103 turned this from a plain-success arrow into a named one. It used to be taken by every reply that was not a declared failure, so a researcher that had settled nothing arrived looking exactly like one that had; now it is taken only when the step says it answered the question, and e06a carries the other case to the same place with that difference visible.

edges.label: the question was not settled
edges.notes: DSP-103. The same destination and the same material as e06 on purpose: an investigation that could not settle the question still belongs back with the step that asked it, together with whatever it did establish, and the implementer is the one that can say whether that is enough to go on with. What differs is that the implementer is told which of the two arrived — and where the researcher named neither, the run routes here and records the outcome as DSpatch's selection rather than the researcher's verdict, so an absence never reads as a finding.

edges.label: could not check
edges.notes: DSP-102. Taken when the verifier did not say that it checked — including when it said so only in prose, which is where the bold BLOCKED of 22 September 2026 went unread. It is not a FAIL: a failing check is still a check, names checked, and goes to the reviewer on e09 with its evidence, because a verdict and an account belong together.

edges.label: rework, bounded
edges.notes:
The rework round, and it returns to the implementer's own agent. maxReworkRounds on the graph is what stops this becoming the same assignment handed to more agents.

The delivers line is DSP-100 and it is why this round is now a round. The implementer's consumes is the brief, so before this the run came back here and handed over the brief again — the identical message, with nothing of the review in it. On 22 September 2026 the implementer read that re-prompt as the answer to the question it had just asked and replied "I understand the clarification", which is not a misreading anyone should be blamed for: nothing else had arrived. The verdict is bound to the visit of implementation-review that produced it, so a third round carries the third review and not the first.

edges.label: could not report a verdict
edges.notes:
DSP-97, and the shared half of it. The destination is e14a's, and the reason is not: what arrives here is a review that could not fulfil the reporting contract this node sets it, which is a different statement from a report step that could not report, and the two are told apart by the edge, by the outcome name and by the node the run came from. The three verdicts are untouched — this is not a fourth way to judge the work, and nothing about accept, rework or needs-decision is decided here.

Before this edge a reviewer that could not answer had nowhere to go: this node declared no failures and stated no fallback, so both the explicit case and the commoner one — a whole review written in prose with no verdict on the line the message asked for — were undeclared products and stopped the run as a runtime fault. The review's own report is filed before this route is chosen, so what it did read and what it could not settle survive the ending.

edges.label: report
edges.notes: DSP-97 turned this from a plain-success arrow into a named one, and that is the whole of the fix at this node. It used to be taken by every reply that was not a declared failure, so a report step that filed a report saying it could not do its own step arrived at an ending whose tick claims the assignment was carried out, verified, reviewed and reported. It is now taken only when the step says it reported, and e14a carries the other case somewhere that says so.

edges.label: could not report
edges.notes:
DSP-97, and the edge the card was filed to decide. Taken where the report step says it could not fulfil its reporting contract, and where its reply names nothing at all — whenUndeclared on the node is what makes the second of those a route rather than a fault at the last step of the run, and the recorded outcome's provenance is what keeps them distinguishable afterwards.

It is not a verdict on the work. Everything before it may have been done, checked and accepted, and on the only path that reaches this node it was: e11 is the sole way in and it is the review's accept. What the ending says is that the run did not report on it, and what the work amounted to is in the earlier steps' own reports and in the working copy, said separately from the ending so that a person can read both. Nothing reads the report body to get here.
